ANTH 25400.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis Department of Anthropology Arch Hoaxes, Myths And Frauds ANTH (WL) 25400 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 3.00. This course examines why the ancient past inspires so many theories about aliens, dark conspiracies, lost civilizations, and apocalyptic predictions. Topics include the popularity of pseudoscientific theories in American culture and the historical contexts in which common pseudoscientific ideas have emerged; why they persist in the face of archaeological evidence; and the role of pseudo-archaeology in the growing antagonism toward scientific expertise. Through an understanding of datasets and methods archaeologists use to evaluate claims about the past, the course goes beyond debunking ancient aliens and Atlantis to develop important critical thinking skills to evaluate evidence and recognize pseudo-scientific arguments in the media. Course Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, you will be able to: Evaluate the difference between a scientific and a pseudoscientific claim about the human past. Explain the techniques and scientific methods archaeologists use for evaluating hypotheses or claims about the past. Examine the role and popularity of pseudoscientific theories in American culture and the historical contexts in which popular pseudoscientific ideas have emerged. Articulate how seemingly harmless fringe theories are entangled with larger narratives of cultural memory and erasure among past societies and their descendants. Learning Resources, Technology & Texts No textbook required Assignments Students will be evaluated based on a combination of short reflection essays on class readings, a group project analyzing a pseudo-archaeological claim in the media, and two exams. BIOL 58601.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis Department of Biological Sciences Ecology BIOL (WL) 58601 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 3.00. This is an advanced ecology course that examines the ecological process and dynamics of populations, communities, and ecosystems. Topics include the physical, physiological, behavioral, and population genetic factors that influence how organisms interact with one another and their environment, the nature of population growth, and attributes of community structure. Course material integrates case studies from field and laboratory experiments, simulations, and theoretical models to understand life histories, species interactions, and community and ecosystem processes. CGT 36500.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis Applied & Creative Computing Game Development Practicum CGT (WL) 36500 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 3.00. This course provides an opportunity for teams of game developers to focus on a project without distraction by competing course deliverables. Students propose a game project and spend the entire semester working only on that project. Course instructors will function as facilitators, producers, and supervisors, helping each student team scaffold their work such that all course goals are met. Prerequisites: Undergraduate level, CGT 20500, Minimum Grade of S Course Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, you will be able to: Decompose a large term game development project into an actionable sequence of smaller development tasks. Face emergent open-ended development challenges and either solve them or adapt to them as project goals require. Set short-term game production goals and consistently meet them. Self-evaluate completed work and iterate as necessary to ensure it meets the project's quality goals. Accept and incorporate criticism regarding one's work and use it to improve one's craft. Deliver criticism constructively that is in service to meeting project quality goals. Maintain group cohesion and morale across a physically separated accordance with industry best productions practices. Internalize and structure individual work habits in accordance with industry best production practices. Required Software / Platforms Current version of Unity or Unreal Engine, depending on the team's project. Microsoft Teams GitHub Jira and/or Confluence, when used by the team or instructor. Assignments Course assessment is based on individual contributions to the team development project and includes seven Sprint Reports, three team project presentations, two Presentation Reflection Reports, and two Game Design Documents. CNIT 27000.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis Applied & Creative Computing Cybersecurity Fundamentals I CNIT (WL) 27000 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 3.00. ECE 20001.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis School of Electrical and Computer Engineering Electrical Engr Fundamentals I ECE (WL) 20001 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 3.00. This course covers fundamental concepts and applications for electrical and computer engineers as well as for engineers who need to gain a broad understanding of these disciplines. The course starts by the basic concepts of charge, current, and voltage as well as their expressions with regards to resistors and resistive circuits. Essential concepts, devices, theorems, and applications of direct-current (DC), 1st order, and alternating-current (AC) circuits are subsequently discussed. Besides electrical devices and circuits, basic electronic components including diodes and transistors as well as their primary applications are also discussed. Assignments Homework Typically, one homework assignment will be distributed every week on Brightspace Lecture Section 2 and will be normally due every Tuesday or Friday 11.59 pm ET . You may bring a self-prepared formula sheet to the exam (one double-sided sheet for the mid-terms, three double-sided sheets for the final) to avoid having to memorize equations. Students will learn how to take their theoretical designs using pen and paper to a physical circuit that has much more structural integrity and reliability than a breadboard. ECE 20007.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis School of Electrical and Computer Engineering Elec Engr Fundamentals I Lab ECE (WL) 20007 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 1.00. This is an introduction course in electronic measurement and circuit modeling, simulation and design techniques. These skills are developed through a variety of laboratory experiments ranging from voltage, current, and frequency, to resistors, inductors, capacitors, and operational amplifiers. When possible, the experiments develop practical skills through small design and soldering tasks. Finally, the course culminates in a two week group design project. In many ways this course is the laboratory of the co-requisite lecture course ECE 20001: Electrical Engineering Fundamentals I; however, we remind students that this is a standalone course that expects students will learn and demonstrate material not taught in ECE 20001. Prerequisites: Undergraduate level, ECE 20001, Minimum Grade of D- [may be taken concurrently] Course Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, you will be able to: Select and use electronic measurement instruments competently. Design, wire, and troubleshoot electronic circuits. Simulate electronic circuits. Keep a laboratory notebook and prepare a formal laboratory report. Function on an interdisciplinary team that draws on diverse backgrounds. Design, build, and test resistor-inductor-capacitor, operational amplifier, etc. circuits to meet specifications. Demonstrate knowledge of laboratory safety precautions. Learning Resources, Technology & Texts No Textbooks required Assignments Lab Notebooks Laboratory notebooks should be a log of all your work performed in this course. This notebook can be either digital or handwritten. If you start with either digital or handwritten, it needs to be consistent throughout the experiment. The notebook should be updated in real time during the experiment. You will use the notebook notes to complete your write-up outside of lab hours. The lab notebook should: • Give a brief context to where you are in the experiment • Capture detailed results from experiment • Give quick/short insights into why you think an outcome occurs The lab notebook is essential for success in this course. It should be kept organized and neat to improve your effectiveness as a researcher. Prelabs For all labs except the first lab, there is a prelab assignment that goes along with the lab. The Prelab Assignment for each lab consists of the following: • Reading the reading portion for that week’s lab • Completing the prelab questions and simulations in your lab notebook • Completing the prelab quiz on Variate (linked through Brightspace) Write-Ups For a majority of the experiments in the course, you will need to turn in a digital version of an experiment write-up. This involves: • Short description of each task including the results of that task • A conclusion of the task based on the results • Answer all questions in the experiments text • Electronically drawn schematics and typed equations Your write-up should be broken up into the tasks of the experiment. For each task you should have: • Objective: 1-2 sentences describing the goal of the task • Digital schematic of the task • The results of that task • Calculations: any calculations needed to be completed for the task • Conclusions: Use the results to identify whether or not an experiment was successful Reports There will be three experiments that require a well-documented formal report to be turned in. These documents will include in paragraph form: • An abstract • An introduction and conclusion to the overall problem and solution • A theory section that explains how the system and its parts work • Contains a discussion of the measurement results and conclusions made based on the results • Has only electronically drawn schematics and typed equations • Answers all question in the experiments text All write-ups and reports need to be completed in a word processor. Handwritten or stylus written write-ups will not be accepted; any handwritten or stylus written component of the writeups and reports will receive a score of 0 for that submission. ECON 25100.text: Purdue West Lafayette/Indianapolis Department of Economics Microeconomics ECON (WL) 25100 WL Fall 2026 Course Description Credit Hours: 3.00. This course is the first formal exposure that students have to the world of microeconomics: the branch of economics that studies the behavior of individuals (people, households, and firms). Topics include scarcity and the economic way of thinking, markets and price determination, elasticity, measuring the value of markets and market interventions, industry structure and outcomes, profit maximization by firms, an introduction to game theory and strategic behavior, and an introduction to international trade. CTL:ISH 1042 Microeconomics Course Learning Outcomes By the end of the course, you will be able to: Identify the core principles and tools used in economic reasoning, including the definition of economics, positive and normative analysis, and the tools of scientific discovery. Apply the market model to describe how the behavior of buyers and sellers determines market outcomes, how interventions in markets affect efficiency, and how markets may fail. Define, measure, calculate, and interpret elasticities and their use in firm decision-making and economic policymaking. Apply the model of consumer choice to describe optimal behavior by consumers. Apply the concept of comparative advantage and market models to describe the potential for gains from trade between agents, including arguments for and against protectionist trade policies between countries. Describe the different types of competitive structures that a firm may operate within and optimal firm decision-making in different competitive structures and in the presence of strategic interactions. The relationship between the structure of materials and the resulting mechanical, thermal, electrical, and optical properties. Applications to design. Perform simple calculations to quantify material properties and microstructural characteristics. Examples: Interplanar spacing of a family of atomic planes given an x-ray diffraction pattern; Equilibrium vacancy concentration at a given temperature; Dimensional changes associated with elastic and plastic deformation; Fracture strength for a given flaw size; Phase composition and fraction using phase diagrams; Apply Reuss and Voight models to determine modulus of composites. Examples: Hall-Petch effect; Dislocation density effect on yield strength and electrical conductivity; Alloying effect on yield strength and electrical conductivity; Inverse relationship between yield strength and fracture toughness; Correlation between type of atomic bonding and the mechanical and electrical properties of different classes of materials. Take information from a known situation and apply it to a new situation. Examples: Effect of temperature and applied stress on the peak positions in an XRD pattern; Simple calculations with multiple steps. Predict property response or microstructural changes based on imposed conditions. Examples: Predicting microstructure using a phase diagram; Predicting microstructure using a TTT diagram; Effects of temperature and alloying on the resistivity of metals. Assess the interplay of two material properties. Examples: Effect of atomic bond strength on Young’s modulus, coefficient of thermal expansion and melting temperature; Determine if a material will yield or rupture at a given applied stress. Identify, formulate, and solve complex materials engineering problems by applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. (10 points) *** Due (9/25) In this two-page reflection essay, you will explore the concept of intersectionality by examining your own identity. Consider how intersecting social categories—such as race, gender, class, nationality, sexuality, religion, or ability—shape your everyday experiences, opportunities, relationships, and worldview. Your goal is not simply to list your identities. Instead, use this essay to reflect on how these identities and social categories interact and shape your life, while also recognizing the unique aspects of yourself that extend beyond any single label.
